required_recommendations: Recognise complete heart block with an infranodal (wide RBBB-morphology) escape as the cause of the syncope and the preceding near-syncope

Admit to a coronary care or monitored bed with transcutaneous pacing pads applied, and temporary transvenous pacing if the escape slows or pauses recur (atropine is unlikely to work with an infranodal escape)
Stop atenolol, but do not delay permanent pacing for drug washout: the wide escape points to infranodal disease, and drug-related AV block often persists after withdrawal (ESC 2021)
Implant a permanent pacing system during this admission (ESC 2021 Class I for third-degree AV block without a reversible cause)

With LVEF 45% and an expected near-complete ventricular pacing burden, choose physiological ventricular pacing (cardiac resynchronisation or conduction-system pacing) rather than right ventricular pacing alone (ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 IIa)

Treat the mildly raised troponin (0.05 ng/mL) with a month of exertional chest tightness after CABG as possible ischaemia: trend it and arrange ischaemia evaluation (coronary and graft angiography if it rises or angina persists)

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: Complete heart block is a Class I indication for permanent pacemaker implantation regardless of symptoms

Beta-blockers must be immediately discontinued in complete heart block without a pacemaker

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Roberto Delgado is a 72-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease status post two-vessel CABG, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and known mild aortic stenosis who presents to the emergency department via EMS after a witnessed syncopal episode at home. The patient was sitting in his recliner watching television at approximately 6:30 PM when he suddenly became pale and slumped to one side, sliding off the chair onto the floor. His wife, who was sitting nearby, states that the episode occurred without any preceding cry, warning, or abnormal movements. She specifically reports that there were no rhythmic jerking movements, no tonic stiffening of the limbs, and no shaking of any kind. She describes him as appearing ashen and motionless for approximately 15 to 20 seconds before he regained consciousness. Upon awakening, he was immediately coherent and oriented, asking his wife why she looked worried. There was no period of confusion, disorientation, or drowsiness after the event, no tongue biting, and no urinary or fecal incontinence. He sustained a small abrasion on his right temple from striking the armrest of the chair. The patient reports that over the past six weeks he has experienced progressive fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, and three prior episodes of near-syncope characterized by a sudden sensation of the room going dark and feeling as though he might lose consciousness, each lasting five to ten seconds and resolving spontaneously. He did not lose consciousness during these prior episodes. He has also noted occasional breathlessness when climbing stairs and vague chest tightness with exertion over the past month, which he attributed to aging. He recalls a minor slip and fall in his bathroom approximately four months ago without loss of consciousness or significant injury, which he mentions as the only prior fall. He denies palpitations immediately before the event, recent fever, headache, visual changes, or focal weakness. His wife confirms he has never had a seizure and that this event looked nothing like a seizure.
